title: A distant conflict is reorganizing domestic safety judgments, identity boundaries, speech restraint, and interfaith cohesion even as most Britons reject a simple partisan side
source_unit: More in Common, Caught between sides: Britons' shifting attitudes to the Israel-Palestine conflict and its consequences at home
geography: United Kingdom, with polling and focus-group evidence on conflict attitudes, Jewish and Muslim safety, media exposure, identity, and community cohesion

observations.period: June and September 2026; reported sympathy and non-alignment

denominator.unit: British public polling respondents; published page does not state the full sample denominator

sympathy_israel.unit: percent saying they sympathise more with the Israeli side

sympathy_palestine.unit: percent saying they sympathise more with the Palestinian side

young_adult_palestine_sympathy.unit: percent of 18-24 year-olds saying they sympathise more with the Palestinian side

non_alignment.value: The largest recent movement was toward saying neither side or being unsure, but the report cautions that this should not be read as indifference.

observations.method: More in Common follow-up research using polling conducted in June 2026, updated sympathy data fielded September 11-15, and a July 2026 focus group; the report compares with its earlier 2025 research.
observations.uncertainty: The publication is a polling and focus-group synthesis with incomplete public sample details in the accessible page; it measures reported attitudes and perceptions, not representative behavioral traces or causal effects of the conflict.
observations.subgroup: British adults, with age and More in Common Seven Segment differences; 18-24 year-olds are a distinctive subgroup in reported Palestinian sympathy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising non-alignment may reflect fatigue, uncertainty, or rejection of binary framing rather than reduced moral or political engagement; sympathy does not establish action, identity change, or policy preference.

observations.period: October 2025-June 2026; conflict stance and social judgment

negative_judgment_of_israel_post.unit: percent saying they would feel worse about someone who posted on social media in support of Israel, up from 27 percent

positive_judgment_of_nonposting.unit: percent saying they would feel better about someone who did not post about the conflict, up from 24 percent

progressive_activist_negative_judgment.unit: percent of Progressive Activists saying they would feel worse about someone posting in support of Israel, up from 45 percent

speech_restraint_mechanism.value: Fear of backlash and feeling under-informed make disengagement or silence appear safer than public commentary.

observations.method: Comparison of More in Common polling waves and focus-group accounts about social-media expression, judgment, and conflict discussion.
observations.uncertainty: Reported social judgments do not measure actual sanctions, platform moderation, employment consequences, or whether silence changes political participation; subgroup movements are descriptive.
observations.subgroup: British adults, including Progressive Activists, young adults, older adults, and other Seven Segments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Avoiding public posting can be a prosocial attempt to lower conflict temperature, not necessarily censorship or political withdrawal; online judgment may not carry into offline relationships.

observations.period: 2024-2026; perceived Jewish and Muslim safety in Britain

safe_for_jewish_people.unit: percent saying the UK is safe for Jewish people, matched by 43 percent saying unsafe

jewish_danger_increase.unit: percent saying it has become more dangerous to be Jewish in the UK

safe_for_muslim_people.unit: percent saying the UK is safe for Muslim people

muslim_danger_increase.unit: percent saying it has become more dangerous to be Muslim in the UK, compared with 20 percent saying less dangerous

safety_consensus_gap.value: Sympathy for Israel or Palestine is associated with sharply different judgments of the other community's safety; the report warns that the direction of causation is unclear.

observations.method: More in Common polling trend comparisons, focus-group accounts, and reported incident context; perceptions are kept separate from incident-record evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived safety is not a direct measure of victimization or community-level risk. The report includes contextual incident claims, but this record does not treat them as a complete hate-crime census or attribute every perception to the conflict.
observations.subgroup: Jewish and Muslim communities in Britain, with age, conflict-sympathy, and Seven Segment differences in perceived safety.
observations.counterinterpretation: Safety judgments may reflect national media attention, local incidents, political identity, or broader crime concerns; a perceived decline does not by itself establish migration, exit, or reduced participation.

observations.period: 2026 report; media/platform exposure and perceived cohesion

social_media_company_safety_performance.unit: percent saying social-media companies are doing enough to make Jews in the UK feel safe

social_media_company_failure.unit: percent saying social-media companies are not doing enough to make Jews in the UK feel safe

media_exposure_vs_everyday_exposure.value: Respondents were more likely to report hearing antisemitic and anti-Muslim comments in media than from friends, family, or colleagues; the gap was especially pronounced for younger respondents.

coexistence_belief.unit: percent believing British Jews and Muslims can live harmoniously while disagreeing about Israel-Palestine, down from 56 percent in October 2025

observations.method: More in Common polling and qualitative conversations on media exposure, platform responsibility, interfaith safety, and social cohesion.
observations.uncertainty: The exposure comparison does not identify specific platforms, content volumes, algorithms, or causal pathways from media exposure to offline hostility; perceived platform responsibility is not a verified moderation audit.
observations.subgroup: British adults, with age and conflict-sympathy differences in reported media exposure and safety judgments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher media recognition may reflect greater visibility or awareness rather than more real-world exposure; declining coexistence belief may be temporary crisis salience rather than durable intergroup separation.

related_sources.claim: More in Common's publication page identifies the report as a September 2026 follow-up on British attitudes to the Israel-Palestine conflict and its domestic social-cohesion effects.
The report provides polling and focus-group findings on sympathy, social judgment, safety for Jewish and Muslim communities, media exposure, platform responsibility, and interfaith coexistence.

boundary: This record adds a geopolitical-to-domestic-cultural route: international conflict salience can shape identity judgment, perceived safety, media exposure, speech restraint, platform accountability, and interfaith-cohesion expectations. It does not establish direct causation, a complete hate-crime count, actual platform behavior, migration or exit, household economic effects, or durable community breakdown.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official More in Common publication page and September 2026 PDF reviewed for fieldwork timing, sympathy, age and segment differences, social judgment, safety perceptions, media exposure, platform responsibility, and coexistence measures.
